text:
### ANC-1.1 Early registration and EDD
- Register every pregnancy as early as possible — **within 12 weeks**, preferably as soon as pregnancy is suspected. Give the woman her MCP card and fill it at every contact.
- Ask the first day of her last menstrual period (LMP).
- Expected date of delivery (EDD): the MoHFW rule is LMP + 9 months + 7 days, which is about 280 days (40 weeks). In the Chandrapuri register and visit list the EDD is always calculated as **LMP + 280 days**. Example: LMP 2026-03-01 → EDD (LMP + 280 days) 2026-12-06.
- Weeks of pregnancy = days since LMP ÷ 7.

### ANC-1.2 Minimum four ANC check-ups
Every pregnant woman should have **at least four ANC check-ups**. This is only a minimum; more visits may be needed.

| Check-up | When |
|---|---|
| 1st | Within 12 weeks (as soon as pregnancy is suspected) |
| 2nd | Between 14 and 26 weeks |
| 3rd | Between 28 and 34 weeks |
| 4th | Between 36 weeks and term |

If a check-up is missed, bring the woman for her next check-up as soon as possible; do not wait for the next window.

### ANC-1.3 PMSMA day (9th of every month)
Under Pradhan Mantri Surakshit Matritva Abhiyan (PMSMA), a check-up by a doctor/specialist is held at government health facilities on the **9th of every month**, for women in the **second or third trimester**. Mobilise every pregnant woman in the second or third trimester to attend at least one PMSMA check-up. High-risk pregnancies found there are tracked.

section_title: What is checked at an ANC check-up
text:
### ANC-1.4 What is checked at an ANC check-up
At each check-up the ANM checks: **weight**, **blood pressure (BP)**, **haemoglobin (Hb)**, **urine for protein and sugar**, and does an abdominal examination for growth of the baby. She also gives IFA, calcium, Td and deworming as due (ANC-2), and counsels on diet, rest, danger signs (ESC-2) and birth preparedness (ANC-5).

## ANC-2 Supplements, deworming and Td in pregnancy

section_title: Folic acid before and in early pregnancy
text:
### ANC-2.1 Folic acid before and in early pregnancy
**400 mcg folic acid** tablet daily during the period before pregnancy (when planning a pregnancy) and up to the end of the **first trimester**.

### ANC-2.2 IFA tablets (iron and folic acid)
- **One Red IFA tablet daily for 180 days**, starting from the **second trimester** of pregnancy. Each tablet contains **60 mg elemental iron + 500 mcg folic acid**.
- After delivery: one Red IFA tablet daily for **180 days** (up to 6 months after delivery).
- Do not take IFA and calcium tablets together: take calcium with meals, and IFA at bedtime or at least two hours after a meal.
- IFA is held during acute illness such as fever, diarrhoea or pneumonia; restart after the illness. For women with thalassemia major or sickle cell disease, iron is decided by the MO.
- Anaemic women get treatment doses (ANC-3.2).

### ANC-2.3 Calcium tablets
- Each tablet: **500 mg elemental calcium + 250 IU vitamin D3**.
- **Twice a day** (total **1 g calcium per day**), starting from **14 weeks of pregnancy** up to **6 months after delivery**.
- Take with meals, never on an empty stomach. Do not take calcium and IFA tablets together, because calcium reduces iron absorption.

### ANC-2.4 Deworming (albendazole) in pregnancy
- **Single dose of albendazole 400 mg** (1 tablet).
- Give it **after the first trimester**, preferably during the second trimester. **Do not give in the first trimester.**

### ANC-2.5 Td vaccine in pregnancy
Td-1 early in pregnancy, Td-2 **4 weeks after Td-1**; only one Td-Booster if she received 2 TT/Td doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years. Full rule: IMM-4.1.

## ANC-3 Anaemia in pregnancy (khoon ki kami)

### ANC-3.1 Hb cut-offs in pregnancy
Anaemia Mukt Bharat (2026) uses these haemoglobin (Hb) cut-offs, in g/dL:

| Trimester | No anaemia | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1st and 3rd trimester | 11.0 or more | 10.0–10.9 | 7.0–9.9 | below 7.0 |
| 2nd trimester | 10.5 or more | 9.5–10.4 | 7.0–9.4 | below 7.0 |

Signs that suggest anaemia: pallor of the inner eyelids, tongue, palms and nails; tiredness; breathlessness on work.

### ANC-3.2 What to do for anaemia
- **Mild or moderate anaemia:** treatment as advised by the ANM/MO is **2 Red IFA tablets daily for 1 month**, then re-test Hb. If Hb has not improved, refer to the FRU/District Hospital.
- **Severe anaemia (Hb below 7 g/dL):** refer the pregnant woman to a higher facility (FRU/District Hospital) — this is a danger sign (ESC-2.5).
- Counsel on iron-rich food (green leafy vegetables, pulses, jaggery, meat/eggs if eaten) and on taking IFA daily.

## ANC-4 High blood pressure in pregnancy

### ANC-4.1 BP 140/90 or more
- Hypertension in pregnancy = systolic BP **140 mmHg or more** and/or diastolic BP **90 mmHg or more** (confirmed on two readings at least 4 hours apart by the ANM/MO).
- A pregnant woman with BP 140/90 or more is a **high-risk pregnancy**: refer her to the Medical Officer the same day; do not wait for the next ANC check-up (ESC-2.3).

### ANC-4.2 Pre-eclampsia and eclampsia
- **Pre-eclampsia** = high BP with protein in the urine. Warning signs: severe headache, blurring of vision, swelling of face/hands or all over the body, pain in the upper abdomen, reduced urine.
- **Eclampsia** = high BP with protein in urine **and convulsions (fits / jhatke)**.
- Any of these is a danger sign: refer immediately (ESC-2.3, ESC-2.2).
- Mild swelling of the feet alone, with normal BP and no other sign, is common in late pregnancy — check BP at the next contact and counsel; it is not by itself a danger sign.

## ANC-5 High-risk pregnancy, birth preparedness and free services

### ANC-5.1 High-risk pregnancy
Some pregnancies need extra care and delivery at a hospital with a doctor (FRU). Conditions tracked as high-risk under PMSMA include: severe anaemia, pregnancy-induced hypertension, gestational diabetes, hypothyroidism, previous caesarean section (LSCS), bad obstetric history or history of stillbirth, twins/multiple pregnancy, teenage pregnancy, elderly or early primi, grand multipara, short stature, cephalo-pelvic disproportion, abnormal foetal heart rate, congenital malformation, negative (Rh) blood group, HIV, syphilis, RTI/STI, hepatitis B, tuberculosis, malaria and high fever. Make sure these women attend PMSMA (ANC-1.3) and plan delivery at a facility that can manage them.

### ANC-5.2 Birth preparedness
Plan in advance: the place of delivery (institutional delivery), transport, money, a companion, and a blood donor. Keep the MCP card ready. Know the ambulance numbers: **102** (free transport for pregnant women and sick infants in most states) and **108** (emergency).

### ANC-5.3 JSSK free services
Under Janani Shishu Suraksha Karyakram (JSSK), pregnant women delivering in government facilities get free: delivery (including caesarean section), drugs, diagnostics, diet and blood; **free transport from home to the health institution**, between facilities in case of referral, and **drop back home after 48 hours** of stay. Sick infants up to 1 year also get free treatment and transport.

### IMM-1.1 Sessions, delays and gaps
- In Chandrapuri Block, routine immunisation sessions are held every **Wednesday and Saturday** at the sub-centre and Anganwadi centres (block arrangement).
- Keep a **minimum gap of 4 weeks** between two doses of the same vaccine (Penta, OPV, RVV). There is no maximum gap: if a child comes late, **do not restart the series** — give the next due dose.
- A child can be vaccinated even if she/he has diarrhoea, mild fever or malnutrition.
- After any vaccine, the child (or woman) should **wait 30 minutes** at the session site.

### IMM-1.2 Due list and tracking
Before each session, the ASHA/ANM prepares a due list of children and pregnant women from the register (see VIS document) and mobilises them. Record every dose with its date on the MCP card and in the register.

## IMM-2 Schedule for infants and children

### IMM-2.1 At birth
| Vaccine | When | Upper limit |
|---|---|---|
| BCG | At birth or as early as possible | till one year of age |
| Hepatitis B birth dose (HepB-0) | At birth | within 24 hours of birth |
| OPV-0 (oral polio, zero dose) | At birth | within the first 15 days |

### IMM-2.2 At 6, 10 and 14 weeks
| Age | Vaccines |
|---|---|
| 6 weeks | OPV-1, Penta-1, RVV-1, fIPV-1, PCV-1 |
| 10 weeks | OPV-2, Penta-2, RVV-2 |
| 14 weeks | OPV-3, Penta-3, RVV-3, fIPV-2, PCV-2 |

- Penta = pentavalent vaccine; RVV = rotavirus vaccine (drops); fIPV = fractional injectable polio vaccine (intradermal, 0.1 ml); PCV = pneumococcal conjugate vaccine.
- OPV can be given till 5 years of age.
- Penta and RVV can be given **till one year of age**. fIPV-1 and fIPV-2 are also given only up to 1 year. If a child over 1 year still has missing Penta or RVV doses, inform the ANM/MO, who decides the catch-up.
- PCV is not started after 1 year. If the child received at least one PCV dose before the first birthday, the remaining PCV doses are completed as early as possible, at least 2 months apart, within the "before 2 years" complete-immunisation window.
- RVV and PCV are now given in all states.

### IMM-2.3 At 9–12 months
- **MR-1** (measles-rubella) at **9 completed months** to 12 months; can be given till 5 years of age.
- **fIPV-3** (third fractional IPV dose) at **9 months**, given together with MR-1 (added to the schedule from 1 January 2023; children who received MR-1 by 31 December 2022 are not called again for fIPV-3).
- **PCV booster (PCV-B)** at 9–12 months (if delayed, completed before 2 years of age — see IMM-2.2).
- **Vitamin A 1st dose** (1 lakh IU, 1 ml) at 9 completed months with MR-1.
- JE-1 only in JE-endemic districts.

### IMM-2.4 At 16–24 months
- **MR-2**, **DPT booster-1 (DPT-B1)**, **OPV booster (OPV-B)**; JE-2 only in endemic districts.
- Give the OPV/DPT booster at least **6 months after OPV-3/Penta-3**. DPT boosters can be given till **7 years of age**.
- **Vitamin A 2nd dose** (2 lakh IU, 2 ml) at 16–18 months, then one dose **every 6 months up to 5 years** of age (9 doses in all).
- If fIPV-3 was missed at 9 months, it can be given with MR-2 at 16–23 months of age, keeping at least 8 weeks after fIPV-2. It is not given after 23 completed months (i.e. not after the second birthday).
- Chandrapuri is **not a JE-endemic district**, so JE vaccine is not given here.

### IMM-2.5 Older children and adolescents
- **DPT booster-2 (DPT-B2)** at **5–6 years**.
- **Td** at **10 years** and at **16 years**.
- **HPV vaccine:** girls who have completed 14 years but not yet 15 years — a **single dose**, given at government health facilities (with cold chain) on routine immunisation days; nationwide roll-out began on 28 February 2026; registration on U-WIN.

### IMM-2.6 Minimum gaps between doses
| Vaccine | Minimum gap between doses |
|---|---|
| Penta, OPV, RVV | 4 weeks |
| PCV | 2 months |
| fIPV | 8 weeks |
| MR-1 to MR-2 (if delayed) | 4 weeks |
| OPV-3/Penta-3 to booster | 6 months |

## IMM-3 After vaccination (AEFI)

### IMM-3.1 Common mild reactions
- Pain, swelling or redness at the injection site, and fever, can occur in about 10% of children (with DPT-containing vaccines in up to half of children). They settle on their own; a cold cloth on the injection site helps. Any medicine is as advised by the ANM/MO.
- BCG: a small swelling appears at the site, may become a small sore, and heals leaving a scar — this is normal.
- MR: mild fever, rash or red eyes can occur in 5–15% of children.
- **Exception:** in a baby **under 2 months** (e.g. after the 6-week vaccines), any fever is a danger sign — follow ESC-4.3.

### IMM-3.2 Reactions to report and refer
Report **immediately** to the ANM (by phone or in person) any high fever, allergic reaction, or **convulsions after immunisation**, and other serious events: persistent screaming, the child becoming limp or unresponsive, difficulty in breathing or swelling of face (anaphylaxis), a large abscess at the injection site, or hospitalisation/death after vaccination. A child with convulsions, breathing difficulty or unresponsiveness after a vaccine must be referred immediately (ESC-5.6).

## IMM-4 Pregnant women

### IMM-4.1 Td in pregnancy
| Dose | When |
|---|---|
| Td-1 | Early in pregnancy (at registration) |
| Td-2 | 4 weeks after Td-1 |
| Td-Booster | If she received 2 TT/Td doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years — then give only one booster dose |

- Td (tetanus and adult diphtheria) replaced TT in the programme in **2018**. Earlier TT doses remain valid; do not restart the series.
- Give Td-2 or the booster preferably before 36 weeks of pregnancy.

### ESC-1.1 Refer immediately
If **even one** danger sign in this document is present, **refer immediately** — the same day, without delay. Do not wait, do not try home treatment first (except the first-aid steps in ESC-1.3), and do not answer the question as a routine one.
- Arrange transport at once: call **108** (emergency ambulance) or **102** (free transport for pregnant women and sick infants under JSSK).
- Take the person to the nearest facility that can manage the problem (PHC/CHC/FRU, or Chandrapuri District Hospital); for newborns the SNCU; for severely malnourished children the NRC (but if a general danger sign is present, the nearest hospital first).
- Inform the ANM and the Medical Officer by phone. Go with the family if possible and carry the MCP card / referral slip.

### ESC-1.2 Check danger signs first
Danger signs are checked **before** anything else. If you are not sure whether a danger sign is present, treat it as present and refer. A sign that has stopped (for example, a fit that is over, or bleeding that has reduced) still needs referral.

### ESC-1.3 While arranging referral
- Newborn: keep the baby warm by skin-to-skin contact with the mother, covered with a cloth, and continue breastfeeding if the baby can suck.
- Person with low sugar who is awake and can swallow: give sugar, misri or a toffee at once (ESC-6.3).
- Do not give anything by mouth to a person who is unconscious or having fits.

### ESC-1.4 Other life-threatening emergencies
Any other emergency that threatens life — for example snakebite, poisoning (pesticide, kerosene or medicines swallowed), severe burns, serious injury, drowning, a person who is unconscious, very drowsy or confused, a diabetes patient whose glucometer shows a very high reading or "HI" together with vomiting, drowsiness or confusion, or someone talking of suicide — also needs you to refer immediately: call 108. Never refuse such a question just because the condition is not covered in these protocols.

## ESC-2 Pregnancy and labour

### ESC-2.1 Bleeding in pregnancy
**Any bleeding from the vagina during pregnancy** (first, second or third trimester), and excessive bleeding during delivery.

### ESC-2.2 Fits or unconsciousness
**Convulsions (fits / jhatke)** or loss of consciousness in a pregnant woman (possible eclampsia).

section_title: High blood pressure and pre-eclampsia signs
text:
### ESC-2.3 High blood pressure and pre-eclampsia signs
- **BP 140/90 or more** in a pregnant woman (ANC-4.1).
- **Severe headache, blurring of vision**, or **swelling of the face and hands / swelling all over the body**, or reduced urine with high BP — signs of pre-eclampsia.

### ESC-2.4 High fever
**High fever during pregnancy or within one month of delivery** — temperature **more than 38 °C** (100.4 °F).

### ESC-2.5 Severe anaemia or breathlessness
- **Hb below 7 g/dL** (severe anaemia), or **severe pallor with or without breathlessness**.
- **Fast or difficult breathing**, or breathlessness at rest.

### ESC-2.6 Severe abdominal pain or vomiting
**Continuous severe abdominal pain**, or **excessive vomiting** — unable to take anything by mouth.

### ESC-2.7 Baby's movements reduced
**Decreased or absent foetal movements** (the baby in the womb is moving less than usual or not at all).

section_title: Water bag, prolonged labour, foul discharge
text:
### ESC-2.8 Water bag, prolonged labour, foul discharge
- **Bursting of the water bag** (leaking watery fluid) **without labour pains**, or before 37 weeks.
- **Labour pain for more than 12 hours.**
- Water bag burst (membranes ruptured) **for more than 18 hours**.
- In labour: **malpresentation** (a hand, foot or cord coming first), **twins / multiple pregnancy**, or **placenta not delivered within 30 minutes** after the birth of the baby.
- **Foul-smelling discharge** from the vagina.

## ESC-3 Mother after delivery (up to 42 days)

### ESC-3.1 Heavy bleeding after delivery
**Heavy bleeding**: a pad is soaked in **less than 5 minutes**, or **more than 5 pads** are changed in a day.

section_title: Fever or foul-smelling discharge after delivery
text:
### ESC-3.2 Fever or foul-smelling discharge after delivery
**High fever within one month of delivery** (temperature more than 38 °C), or **foul-smelling discharge with fever**. (The HBNC home-visit form uses 102 °F for fever alone; this protocol uses the stricter 38 °C from the MCP card and the 2010 ANC guidelines.)

section_title: Fits, abnormal behaviour or severe headache after delivery
text:
### ESC-3.3 Fits, abnormal behaviour or severe headache after delivery
**Fits**, speaking or behaving abnormally, loss of consciousness, or severe headache with blurring of vision.

section_title: Breathlessness, pallor or abdominal pain after delivery
text:
### ESC-3.4 Breathlessness, pallor or abdominal pain after delivery
After delivery (up to 42 days): **fast or difficult breathing** or **breathlessness at rest**, **severe pallor** (severe anaemia), or **continuous severe abdominal pain**.

## ESC-4 Newborn and young infant (up to 2 months)

### ESC-4.1 Feeding, cry and activity
- **Feeding less or stopped / unable to suck** at the breast.
- **Cry weak or stopped.**
- **All limbs limp**, or the baby is **lethargic or unconscious**.
- **Convulsions (fits).**

### ESC-4.2 Breathing
- Breathing **60 per minute or more** (count for one full minute).
- **Chest indrawing**, difficulty in breathing, or blue tongue and lips.

### ESC-4.3 Temperature
- Baby has fever: feels hot, or temperature **more than 99 °F (37.2 °C)** on the HBNC thermometer check.
- Baby is **cold to touch**, or temperature **below 95.9 °F (35.5 °C)**.
- The newborn fever cut-off (more than 99 °F, from the HBNC home-visit form) is deliberately lower than the 37.5 °C used for older children in CHD-2.1.

### ESC-4.4 Other newborn danger signs
- **Pus or redness of the umbilicus**, or bleeding from the cord.
- **10 or more skin pustules**, or a big boil.
- **Jaundice on the first day**, **yellow palms and soles**, or jaundice that persists after 14 days.
- **Distended abdomen**, or the baby vomits often.
- **Blood in the stool.**
- **Weight less than 1.8 kg** (refer to SNCU).

## ESC-5 Child 2 months to 5 years

### ESC-5.1 General danger signs
- **Not able to drink or breastfeed.**
- **Vomits everything.**
- **Convulsions (fits)** now or during this illness.
- **Lethargic or unconscious.**

section_title: Cough with fast breathing or chest indrawing
text:
### ESC-5.2 Cough with fast breathing or chest indrawing
Cough or difficult breathing **with fast breathing** (**50 per minute or more** at 2–12 months; **40 per minute or more** at 12 months–5 years), **chest indrawing**, or **stridor** (harsh noise on breathing in) in a calm child.

### ESC-5.3 Diarrhoea danger signs
- **Severe dehydration** — two of: lethargic or unconscious; sunken eyes; not able to drink or drinking poorly; skin pinch goes back very slowly (longer than 2 seconds).
- **Blood in the stools.**
- **Diarrhoea for 14 days or more.**
- Diarrhoea in a child with **severe malnutrition** (refer to NRC even without dehydration).

### ESC-5.4 Fever danger signs
- Fever with **any general danger sign** (ESC-5.1) or a **stiff neck**.
- **Fever every day for more than 7 days.**

### ESC-5.5 Severe acute malnutrition with complications
Refer immediately to the **NRC** if a child has **oedema of both feet**, or SAM (MUAC below 11.5 cm) together with any of: poor appetite (fails the appetite test), visible severe wasting, severe palmar pallor, lethargy or drowsiness, continual irritability, any breathing difficulty, or signs of severe dehydration. Any infant under 6 months who is **visibly wasted, has oedema, or is too weak to suckle** must also be referred immediately.

### ESC-5.6 Serious reaction after vaccination
**Convulsions**, breathing difficulty or swelling of the face, the child becoming **limp or unresponsive**, or persistent screaming after a vaccine. Refer immediately and report to the ANM at once (IMM-3.2).

### ESC-5.7 Severe palmar pallor
**Severe palmar pallor** (palms very pale/white) in a child — possible severe anaemia.

## ESC-6 Adults with hypertension or diabetes

### ESC-6.1 Heart attack signs
**Any pain, pressure or tightness in the centre of the chest**, especially with sweating, shortness of breath, nausea, or pain spreading to the jaw, neck, arms, shoulders or back, or unconsciousness → refer immediately to the CHC/hospital (call 108). Do not wait to see whether the pain passes. People with diabetes may have a heart attack with little or no pain.

### ESC-6.2 Stroke signs (BE FAST)
**Sudden weakness, paralysis or numbness of the face, arm or leg on one side**, **loss of speech or difficulty speaking**, sudden dimness or loss of vision, sudden dizziness, unsteadiness or falls, or a sudden severe headache or loss of consciousness → refer immediately. BE FAST = Balance, Eyes, Face, Arm, Speech, Time.

### ESC-6.3 Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia)
A diabetes patient with sweating, tremors, confusion, fast heartbeat, dizziness or blurred vision may have low sugar (**below 70 mg/dl**). If awake and able to swallow, give **sugar, misri or a toffee at once** (first aid, ESC-1.3), then send the person to the Medical Officer the same day, because low sugar in a person on diabetes medicines can come back. If the person is **unconscious, having fits, or does not improve** after the sugar, refer immediately (call 108).

### ESC-6.4 Very high blood pressure
**BP 180/110 or more** (systolic 180 or more, or diastolic 110 or more), even without any complaint, is an escalation: refer the person to the Medical Officer the same day — the MO starts treatment and refers to a specialist (NCD-1.2). If it comes with severe headache, chest pain, breathlessness, confusion or weakness of one side, call 108 and refer immediately (ESC-6.1, ESC-6.2).

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-1.1 HBNC visit schedule
| Place of delivery | Number of home visits | Visit days |
|---|---|---|
| Institutional delivery | 6 visits | Days 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 |
| Home delivery | 7 visits | Days 1, 3, 7, 14, 21, 28 and 42 |

- The day of birth is day 1. For a baby born at home, the first visit is on the day of birth.
- After a caesarean delivery, visits start from day 7 (because mother and baby stay longer in hospital).
- At every visit check both the **baby** (HBNC-1.3) and the **mother** (HBNC-3).

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-1.2 Low birth weight babies
- **Low birth weight (LBW) = birth weight less than 2.5 kg.** These babies need special care: extra warmth (skin-to-skin), more frequent breastfeeding, and three extra home visits (MCP card).
- A baby weighing **less than 1.8 kg** must be referred to the SNCU (sick newborn care unit) — see ESC-4.4.
- LBW babies and babies discharged from SNCU get follow-up visits in the 3rd, 6th, 9th and 12th month (NHSRC HBNC/HBYC handbook).

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
section_title: What to check in the baby at each visit
text:
### HBNC-1.3 What to check in the baby at each visit
Feeding (is the baby sucking well?), cry, activity (is the baby limp?), breathing rate (count for one full minute) and chest indrawing, temperature, umbilical cord (pus, redness, bleeding), skin (pustules), eyes, jaundice (yellow skin, palms, soles), stools and vomiting, weight. Any danger sign → refer immediately (ESC-4).

## HBNC-2 Essential newborn care advice

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-2.1 Breastfeeding
- Start breastfeeding **within 1 hour of birth**.
- **Exclusive breastfeeding for 6 months**: only breast milk — no water, honey, ghutti, animal milk or anything else.
- Feed on demand, day and night; give the first yellow milk (colostrum).

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
section_title: Keeping the baby warm and bathing
text:
### HBNC-2.2 Keeping the baby warm and bathing
- Keep the baby warm: skin-to-skin contact with the mother (Kangaroo Mother Care), cover the head, hands and feet, keep the baby with the mother.
- If the baby's temperature is below 97 °F, warm the baby by skin-to-skin contact and check again after about 1 hour; if it is still below 97 °F, refer. A baby who is cold to touch, or whose temperature is below 95.9 °F (35.5 °C), is in danger (ESC-4.3).
- **Do not bathe the baby for the first 48 hours.** Do not bathe a low birth weight baby until its weight is 2000 g; clean with a soft, warm, wet cloth instead.

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-2.3 Cord care
- **Do not apply anything on the cord** (no oil, ash, cow dung, powder or ointment). Keep the cord and umbilicus clean and dry.

## HBNC-3 Care of the mother after delivery (postnatal care)

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-3.1 Mother's check and supplements
- At each visit ask about bleeding (how many pads changed in a day), fever, foul-smelling discharge, pain, breast problems, fits or abnormal talk. Danger signs → refer immediately (ESC-3).
- Continue **one Red IFA tablet daily for 180 days** after delivery and **calcium (two tablets a day) up to 6 months** after delivery (ANC-2.2, ANC-2.3).
- Counsel on nutritious diet, rest, breastfeeding, and family planning methods (refer to ANM for a method).

## HBNC-4 Home-Based Young Child Care (HBYC)

doc_title: HBNC — Home-Based Newborn Care and Postnatal Care
text:
### HBNC-4.1 HBYC visits
After HBNC ends, the ASHA makes **five HBYC home visits in the 3rd, 6th, 9th, 12th and 15th month** of the child's life — to check growth, immunisation, exclusive breastfeeding until 6 months, start of complementary feeding at 6 months, ORS and zinc use, and play/communication.

## Sources
- MoHFW, *Revised Home Based Newborn Care Operational Guidelines* (2014): https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/child-health/guidelines/Revised_Home_Based_New_Born_Care_Operational_Guidelines_2014.pdf — 6/7 visits and days, caesarean start day 7.
- NHSRC, *Handbook for ASHA Facilitators and ANM/MPW on HBNC and HBYC*: https://nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2022-02/Handbook%20for%20ASHA%20Facilitators%20and%20MPWs%20on%20HBNC%20and%20HBYC.pdf — HBNC form (pads per day, temperature cut-offs, <1.8 kg refer, LBW care), HBYC 3/6/9/12/15 months, LBW/SNCU follow-up months.
- MoHFW, *Guidelines for Antenatal Care and Skilled Attendance at Birth* (2010): https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/maternal-health/guidelines/sba_guidelines_for_skilled_attendance_at_birth.pdf — breastfeeding within one hour, exclusive breastfeeding 6 months, nothing on the cord.
- MCP card (MoHFW/NHM): https://nhm.gov.in/New_Updates_2018/NHM_Components/Immunization/Guildelines_for_immunization/MCP_Card_English_version.pdf — LBW < 2.5 kg special care and three extra visits; do not bathe for first 48 hours.
- MoHFW, *IMNCI Chart Booklet* (2023): low body temperature — warm and reassess after 1 hour: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/child-health/guidelines/IMNCI-Module-2023-For-Medical-Officers/IMNCI-Chart-booklet-Medical-Officer-2023.pdf
- NHSRC, *ASHA Module 7 — Skills that Save Lives*: https://nhsrcindia.org/sites/default/files/2021-06/Skills%20That%20Save%20Lives%20ASHA%20Module-7%20English.pdf — do not bathe a baby until weight is 2000 g.
- Anemia Mukt Bharat Operational Guidelines (2026) and Calcium guidelines (2014) — see ANC document.

### NUT-1.1 Who and how
- Screen **all children 6–59 months** with the MUAC tape (mid-upper arm circumference) and look for **bilateral pitting oedema** (oedema of both feet).
- MUAC is used only for children **6 months or older**. Infants under 6 months are not measured with MUAC (see NUT-2.4).
- Oedema check: press gently on the top of both feet; if a dent (pit) remains in **both** feet, the child has bilateral pitting oedema.
- In Chandrapuri Block, MUAC is re-measured every month by the ASHA/AWW (block arrangement; VIS-5.2).

### NUT-1.2 MUAC classification (children 6–59 months)
| Result | MUAC | Colour on the tape |
|---|---|---|
| Severe acute malnutrition (SAM) | **below 11.5 cm**, or **oedema of both feet** at any MUAC | red |
| Moderate acute malnutrition (MAM) | **11.5–12.4 cm** | yellow |
| No acute malnutrition | **12.5 cm or more** | green |

SAM is also diagnosed by the ANM/MO when weight-for-height is below −3 SD.

## NUT-2 What to do

### NUT-2.1 SAM with complications → NRC immediately
A SAM child with **any** complication — poor appetite (fails the appetite test), visible severe wasting, **oedema of both feet**, severe palmar pallor, lethargy/drowsiness/unconsciousness, continual irritability, any breathing difficulty, or signs of severe dehydration — must be referred **immediately** to the Nutrition Rehabilitation Centre (NRC). See ESC-5.5.

### NUT-2.2 SAM without complications
A SAM child (MUAC below 11.5 cm) who is alert, has no oedema and no other complication must be taken to the ANM/CHO/Medical Officer for a **medical check and appetite test**. Children who **fail the appetite test** are referred to the NRC; children who pass are managed in the community under the CMAM protocol, with regular follow-up by the AWW/ASHA.

### NUT-2.3 MAM
For a child with MAM (MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm): counsel the family on feeding (more frequent, energy-dense meals and continued breastfeeding), make sure the child gets supplementary nutrition from the Anganwadi centre, check for illness and immunisation, and re-measure MUAC every month.

### NUT-2.4 Infants under 6 months
Do not use MUAC. Any infant under 6 months who is **visibly wasted**, has **oedema**, or is **too weak or feeble to suckle** must be referred immediately (ESC-5.5). Support exclusive breastfeeding.

### NUT-2.5 Feeding advice to prevent malnutrition
Exclusive breastfeeding for the first 6 months; start complementary food at 6 months while continuing breastfeeding; feed extra during and after illness.

## Sources
- MoHFW, *IMNCI Chart Booklet for Medical Officers* (2023): SAM = WFL < −3 SD and/or MUAC < 11.5 cm and/or oedema of both feet; MAM = MUAC 11.5–12.4 cm; no acute malnutrition = MUAC ≥ 12.5 cm; MUAC only if 6 months or older: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/child-health/guidelines/IMNCI-Module-2023-For-Medical-Officers/IMNCI-Chart-booklet-Medical-Officer-2023.pdf
- MoHFW, *Operational Guidelines on Facility Based Management of Children with SAM* (2011): screening of all children 6–59 months by AWW/ASHA with MUAC tape and for bilateral pitting oedema; community referral flow chart: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/child-health/guidelines/operational_guidelines_on_fbmc_with_sam.pdf
- MoWCD & MoHFW, *Protocol for Management of Malnutrition in Children (CMAM)* (October 2023): appetite test; failures and complicated SAM to NRC; infants under 6 months: https://www.spniwcd.wcd.gov.in/uploads/pdf/CMAM-Book-10-10-2023%20(1).pdf
- Colour bands (red/yellow/green) follow the standard colour-coded MUAC tape used in the programme.
- Monthly MUAC re-measurement in Chandrapuri: block arrangement for this hackathon.

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
section_title: Who is screened and how often
text:
### NCD-1.1 Who is screened and how often
- All women and men aged **30 years and above** are screened for hypertension and diabetes **once a year**, whatever their CBAC score.
- The ASHA fills the **CBAC form** (Community Based Assessment Checklist). A **score above 4** means the person may be at higher risk and should be **prioritised** for screening.

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
text:
### NCD-1.2 BP screening and referral
- Hypertension = systolic BP **140 mmHg or more** and/or diastolic BP **90 mmHg or more**, found on **two different occasions**.
- A person whose screening BP is 140/90 or more is referred to the **Medical Officer** (PHC / Ayushman Arogya Mandir) to confirm the diagnosis and start treatment. This is a routine referral, not an emergency — unless the BP is 180/110 or more (then escalate: same-day referral, ESC-6.4) or danger signs are present (ESC-6).
- For the MO's information: 140–159 / 90–99 → check again on another day; 160–179 / 100–109 → second reading the same day and start treatment the same day; **180 or more / 110 or more** → start treatment and refer to a specialist.

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
text:
### NCD-1.3 Blood sugar screening and referral
- A random blood sugar by glucostrip of **140 mg/dl or more** is a suspected diabetes case → refer to the **Medical Officer** for confirmation.
- Diagnosis is made by the MO: fasting **126 mg/dl or more**, or 2-hour post-meal 200 mg/dl or more, or HbA1c 6.5% or more, or random 200 mg/dl or more with symptoms of diabetes.

## NCD-2 Follow-up of known patients

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
text:
### NCD-2.1 Monthly follow-up
- The ASHA visits every known hypertension/diabetes patient **every month** to check that medicines are being taken, support diet and lifestyle change, and encourage the patient to get **BP and blood sugar measured every month**.
- Medicines are **refilled monthly** at the PHC / Ayushman Arogya Mandir.
- If BP is still **140/90 or more**, or sugar stays high, the condition is not controlled → refer to the Medical Officer for review. Exception: if BP is **180/110 or more**, this is an escalation — refer the same day (ESC-6.4).
- Each patient should be reviewed by a doctor/specialist **at least once a year**.

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
text:
### NCD-2.2 Medicines
- Patients must **not stop their medicines** on their own, even when they feel well or the reading is normal.
- The ASHA does **not** start, stop or change the dose of any BP or diabetes medicine or insulin — that is decided only by the Medical Officer (SCP-1.2).

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
section_title: Low blood sugar in diabetes patients
text:
### NCD-2.3 Low blood sugar in diabetes patients
- Low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) = **below 70 mg/dl**.
- Signs: tremors, sweating, nervousness, irritability, confusion, fast heartbeat, dizziness, hunger, blurred vision, headache, weakness; in severe cases fits or unconsciousness.
- Action: give **sugar, misri or a toffee** at once if the person is awake. Advise diabetes patients to always carry sugar, misri or toffee. Unconscious, fits or not improving → refer immediately (ESC-6.3).

## NCD-3 Healthy lifestyle advice

doc_title: NCD — Hypertension and Diabetes: Screening and Follow-up
text:
### NCD-3.1 Lifestyle counselling
- Salt: a **maximum of 1 teaspoon (5 g) of salt** for the whole day, including salt in cooking; avoid pickles, papad and packaged salty snacks.
- Physical activity: **at least 30 minutes** of regular activity for **at least 5 days a week** (150 minutes a week).
- Stop tobacco (bidi, cigarette, gutkha, khaini) and avoid alcohol.
- Eat more fruits, vegetables and whole grains; keep a healthy weight.

## Sources
- MoHFW, *NP-NCD Operational Guidelines 2023–2030* (PBS for 30 years and above; hypertension ≥140 and/or ≥90 on two occasions; MO BP bands; glucostrip 140 mg/dl; diagnosis criteria; monthly refill; uncontrolled → MO; annual review): archived copy of https://www.mohfw.gov.in/sites/default/files/NP-NCD%20Operational%20Guidelines_0.pdf (via web.archive.org).
- MoHFW, *Operational Guidelines on Prevention, Screening and Control of Common NCDs* (2016) (annual screening for hypertension and diabetes; monthly ANM/ASHA visits; RBS 140 mg/dl and above → MO): archived copy from main.mohfw.gov.in.
- NHM/AAM, *Module for ASHA on Non-Communicable Diseases* (annual screening 30+; CBAC score above 4; monthly BP and glucose; salt 5 g; 30 minutes 5 days a week; hypoglycaemia below 70 mg/dl, signs, misri/toffee): https://aam.mohfw.gov.in/download/document/263f3ca26df87dc44b7687c1b9cf0c15.pdf
- Note: the 2023 NP-NCD main text describes the CBAC cut-off as "4 or more", while the CBAC form says "above 4"; this document follows the form.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.1 Preparing ORS
- Mix **1 packet of ORS in 1 litre** of clean drinking water (boiled and cooled), in a clean container.
- **Throw away ORS solution after 24 hours** and make fresh.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.2 How much ORS to give
| Age | ORS after each loose stool |
|---|---|
| Up to 2 years | **50 to 100 ml** |
| 2 years or more | **100 to 200 ml** |

- Give frequent small sips from a cup (or spoon). If the child vomits, **wait 10 minutes**, then continue more slowly.
- Continue giving extra fluid until the diarrhoea stops. Give the mother **2 packets of ORS** to use at home.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.3 Zinc
| Age | Zinc dose (20 mg tablet) |
|---|---|
| 2 months up to 6 months | **half tablet (10 mg)** once a day |
| 6 months up to 5 years | **one full tablet (20 mg)** once a day |

- Give zinc for **14 days**, **even if the diarrhoea stops** earlier.
- Dissolve the tablet in a spoon of breast milk (for 2–6 months) or clean water (older children).
- Zinc is **not given to infants under 2 months**; a young infant with diarrhoea should be seen by the ANM/MO.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.4 Feeding during diarrhoea
**Continue feeding, including breastfeeding**, during diarrhoea, and give **extra feeds during and after the illness**. Do not stop food or breast milk.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.5 Checking for dehydration
| Classification | Signs |
|---|---|
| Severe dehydration | **two** of: lethargic or unconscious; sunken eyes; not able to drink or drinking poorly; skin pinch goes back **very slowly** (longer than 2 seconds) |
| Some dehydration | two of: restless, irritable; sunken eyes; drinks eagerly, thirsty; skin pinch goes back slowly |
| No dehydration | not enough signs for the above |

- **No dehydration:** ORS + zinc + feeding at home (CHD-1.2 to CHD-1.4).
- **Some dehydration:** the child needs ORS treatment under the supervision of the ANM/health facility (IMNCI Plan B); give ORS on the way.
- **Severe dehydration:** refer urgently (ESC-5.3).

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-1.6 When to return or refer
Tell the mother to come back or go to the health facility **immediately** if the child becomes sicker, is not able to drink or breastfeed, is drinking poorly, has **blood in the stool**, or develops a fever. Blood in stool, diarrhoea for 14 days or more, or diarrhoea in a severely malnourished child → refer (ESC-5.3).

## CHD-2 Fever (bukhar) in children

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-2.1 What counts as fever
Fever = the child feels hot (or has fever by history), or temperature **37.5 °C (99.5 °F) or above**. Always look for danger signs first (ESC-5.1, ESC-5.4); in a baby under 2 months see ESC-4.3.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
section_title: When a child with fever must be referred
text:
### CHD-2.2 When a child with fever must be referred
- Fever with **any general danger sign** (not able to drink or breastfeed, vomits everything, convulsions, lethargic or unconscious) or a **stiff neck** → refer urgently (ESC-5.4).
- Fever present **every day for more than 7 days** → refer for assessment.

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-2.3 Malaria and medicines
- In malaria-prone areas, a child with fever and no obvious other cause is tested for malaria (RDT) as per the national programme; treatment is given as per national guidelines by trained staff.
- The choice and dose of any medicine for fever or infection — **including paracetamol** and antibiotics — is decided by the ANM/Medical Officer; drug dosing is **out of scope** for this assistant (SCP-1.2).
- At home: keep giving fluids and breastfeeding, and come back if the child becomes sicker.

## CHD-3 Cough and fast breathing

doc_title: CHD — Childhood Illness: Diarrhoea (ORS + Zinc), Fever, Fast Breathing
text:
### CHD-3.1 Counting breaths
Count the child's breaths for **one full minute** when the child is calm. Fast breathing is:

| Age | Fast breathing |
|---|---|
| Under 2 months | 60 breaths per minute or more |
| 2 months up to 12 months | **50 breaths per minute or more** |
| 12 months up to 5 years | **40 breaths per minute or more** |

A child with cough or difficult breathing **and** fast breathing, or with **chest indrawing** or **stridor** (a harsh noise when breathing in) when calm, must be referred (ESC-5.2; for babies under 2 months ESC-4.2).

## Sources
- MoHFW, *IMNCI Chart Booklet for Medical Officers* (2023): ORS 50–100 ml (up to 2 years) and 100–200 ml (2 years or more) after each loose stool; small sips, wait 10 minutes after vomiting; 2 packets of ORS; zinc table from 2 months; dehydration classification; fever 37.5 °C/99.5 °F; general danger signs; fever more than 7 days; fast-breathing cut-offs; RDT: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/programmes/child-health/guidelines/IMNCI-Module-2023-For-Medical-Officers/IMNCI-Chart-booklet-Medical-Officer-2023.pdf
- MoHFW, *IDCF Operational Guidelines* (2017): zinc for 14 days even if diarrhoea stops; continue feeding; when to return: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/IDCF-2017/IDCF_guidelines_2017.pdf
- MoHFW, *IDCF Toolkit* (2019): zinc 10 mg (2–6 months) / 20 mg (6 months–5 years), dissolve in breast milk or water; discard ORS after 24 hours; urgent referral list: https://nhm.goa.gov.in/wp-content/uploads/2020/06/IDCF_Toolkit_3-April-2019.pdf
- NHM, *ASHA Module 7* (older edition): ORS preparation in 1 litre of drinking water: https://nhm.gov.in/images/pdf/communitisation/asha/book-no-7.pdf
- Note: older ASHA module ORS volumes differ; this document follows IMNCI 2023.

doc_title: SCP — Scope of This Assistant and When to Redirect
text:
### SCP-1.1 Covered topics
The assistant answers only from these protocol documents: antenatal care (ANC), immunisation (IMM), danger signs and referral (ESC), newborn and postnatal home visits (HBNC), malnutrition screening (NUT), hypertension and diabetes screening and follow-up (NCD), diarrhoea, fever and fast breathing in children (CHD), and the daily visit list (VIS). Every answer must name the protocol section it comes from (for example "ANC-1.2").

doc_title: SCP — Scope of This Assistant and When to Redirect
section_title: Not covered — redirect to the doctor

doc_title: SCP — Scope of This Assistant and When to Redirect
text:
### SCP-1.3 How to answer
- Check danger signs first (ESC-1.2). If a danger sign is present, say **refer immediately** before anything else.
- Keep answers short and practical, in the worker's language, and keep numbers exactly as written in the protocol.
- Never guess a number or a dose. If the protocol does not say it, say so and redirect (SCP-1.2).

## Sources
- Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PC-PNDT) Act, 1994 (prohibition of sex selection): https://pndt.mohfw.gov.in/
- Scope rules for this hackathon assistant, based on the division of roles in the MoHFW ASHA/ANM training material cited in the other documents (ASHAs counsel, screen, follow up and refer; prescribing and diagnosis are done by the Medical Officer).

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-1.1 Purpose
Every morning the ASHA/ANM makes a list of household members who need a visit or a service: who is due for what, and which visits come first. The list is made from the household register for one day ("today"). For this hackathon, today is **2026-10-26 (Monday)**. The register contains everything recorded up to the evening of 2026-10-25.

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-1.2 Status of an item
Each item on the list has one status:
- **overdue** — the item was due and its allowed time has passed without it being done.
- **due_today** — the item is due now: its due date has arrived and it is still within its allowed time.
- **due_this_week** — the item will become due in the next 6 days (2026-10-27 to 2026-11-01). Plan it now.

Note that "overdue" depends on the item: ANC is overdue the day after its window closes (VIS-2.1), an HBNC visit the day after its visit day (VIS-4.1), and all other items more than 28 days after their due date (VIS-1.3).

Items that become due later than 6 days from today are **not** listed.

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-1.3 Counting conventions [block rule]

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| upcoming_horizon_days | 6 |
| grace_days | 28 |
| followup_interval_days | 30 |
| td2_gap_days | 28 |
| vaccine_list_age_to_days | 2554 |
| hbnc_age_to_days | 42 |
| muac_age_from_days | 184 |
| muac_age_to_days | 1824 |

- All ages and gaps are counted in **days**. Age in days = today minus date of birth.
- Calendar ages are converted to days so that an item is **never listed before** the child completes that age: 6 weeks = 42 days, 10 weeks = 70, 14 weeks = 98, 6 months = 184, 9 completed months = 276, 16 months = 490, 5 years = 1827. The "not after" ages in VIS-3.1 are the last age (in days) at which a dose may still be listed: 365 (1 year), 1825 (5 years) and 2554 (just under 7 years). Follow-up intervals use 30 days for one month.
- **grace_days**: a vaccine, Td dose, MUAC check or NCD follow-up is **overdue** when today is more than 28 days after its due date (four weekly session cycles missed). On day 28 after the due date it is still due_today. Every "becomes overdue 28 days after its due date" in this document means this.
- **followup_interval_days**: MUAC re-check and NCD (BP / sugar) follow-up are due 30 days after the last recorded check.
- Children are on the vaccine part of the list while their age is 0 to 2554 days (under 7 years, the upper age for DPT boosters).
- The list starts from what is recorded in the register. A **new** danger sign found during any visit is never left for the list: refer immediately (ESC-1.1).

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-1.4 Messy register entries
The register is filled by hand. Vaccine codes may be written in different ways (for example `penta1`, `PENTA 1`, `Penta-1` all mean Penta-1). A blood-pressure reading of `0/0` or a blank cell means the reading was not recorded (a check date in its own column still counts as a check). A blank date means "not recorded". Duplicate vaccine entries count once (use the earliest date).

## VIS-2 Pregnant women

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-2.1 ANC check-ups
ANC check-ups are numbered in the order they happen: the first recorded check-up is ANC-1, the second is ANC-2, and so on (see ANC-1.2 for the timing). The next check-up due is number (check-ups done + 1). It is due from the day the pregnancy reaches the start of its window, and it is **overdue** after the end of its window. Days are counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP).

| Item | Opens (days since LMP) | Closes (days since LMP) |
|---|---|---|
| ANC-1 | 0 | 84 |
| ANC-2 | 98 | 182 |
| ANC-3 | 196 | 238 |
| ANC-4 | 252 | 280 |

(84 days = 12 weeks; 98 = 14 weeks; 182 = 26 weeks; 196 = 28 weeks; 238 = 34 weeks; 252 = 36 weeks; 280 days = 40 weeks = the expected date of delivery, EDD = LMP + 280 days.) After 4 check-ups no ANC item is listed. The whole open window counts as due_today. A woman still recorded as pregnant after her EDD keeps her next missing ANC check-up (whatever its number) as overdue — inform the ANM.

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-2.2 Td in pregnancy
- If the woman is **booster-eligible** (`td_booster_eligible = Y`: two TT/Td doses in a pregnancy within the last 3 years, see IMM-4.1), she needs only **Td-BST**. Otherwise she needs **Td-1** and **Td-2**.
- Td-1 (or Td-BST) is due on the date of her first recorded ANC check-up. If she has no ANC check-up yet, Td is not listed separately (ANC-1 is listed instead).
- Td-2 is due 28 days after the date Td-1 was actually given (listed only once Td-1 is recorded).
- Each Td item becomes overdue 28 days after its due date (grace_days). Td items are listed while she is recorded as pregnant.

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-2.3 High-risk pregnancy follow-up [block rule]
Every pregnant woman whose last recorded Hb is below 7 g/dL or whose last ANC BP is 140/90 or more was referred at that ANC check-up (ESC-2.3, ESC-2.5). She gets the item **HRP-followup** on every day's list, with status **due_today** (and therefore priority 1): visit her, confirm that the referral to the MO/FRU was completed, and check for danger signs.

## VIS-3 Children: vaccines

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-3.1 Vaccine due rules
A dose is listed when: the child has not had it; the "previous dose needed" (if any) has been given; and the child is not past the "not after" age. Its due date is the later of (date of birth + due age) and (date of previous dose + minimum gap). It becomes overdue 28 days after its due date, or on the day the child reaches the "not after" age, whichever is earlier. Doses past the "not after" age are not listed — tell the ANM, who decides on catch-up. A dose whose due date (after adding the minimum gap) falls after its "not after" age is also not listed. In the table, "-" in the "not after" column means no limit other than the vaccine-list age (2554 days); "-" in the gap column means no minimum gap; "-" in the previous-dose column means none needed. The ages come from IMM-2.

| Item | Due from age (days) | Not after age (days) | Previous dose needed | Minimum gap after previous dose (days) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| BCG | 0 | 365 | - | - |
| HepB-0 | 0 | 0 | - | - |
| OPV-0 | 0 | 15 | - | - |
| OPV-1 | 42 | 1825 | - | - |
| OPV-2 | 70 | 1825 | OPV-1 | 28 |
| OPV-3 | 98 | 1825 | OPV-2 | 28 |
| Penta-1 | 42 | 365 | - | - |
| Penta-2 | 70 | 365 | Penta-1 | 28 |
| Penta-3 | 98 | 365 | Penta-2 | 28 |
| RVV-1 | 42 | 365 | - | - |
| RVV-2 | 70 | 365 | RVV-1 | 28 |
| RVV-3 | 98 | 365 | RVV-2 | 28 |
| fIPV-1 | 42 | 365 | - | - |
| fIPV-2 | 98 | 365 | fIPV-1 | 56 |
| fIPV-3 | 276 | 729 | fIPV-2 | 56 |
| PCV-1 | 42 | 365 | - | - |
| PCV-2 | 98 | 729 | PCV-1 | 60 |
| PCV-B | 276 | 729 | PCV-2 | 60 |
| MR-1 | 276 | 1825 | - | - |
| MR-2 | 490 | 1825 | MR-1 | 28 |
| OPV-B | 490 | 1825 | OPV-3 | 180 |
| DPT-B1 | 490 | 2554 | Penta-3 | 180 |
| DPT-B2 | 1827 | 2554 | DPT-B1 | - |

"-" means no limit within this list (the child stays on the vaccine list until 2554 days of age). Upper ages follow IMM-2: Penta, RVV, fIPV-1/2 and PCV-1 only up to 1 year (365 days); PCV-2, PCV-B and fIPV-3 only before 2 years (729 days; fIPV-3 catch-up is at 16–23 months, and it exists only since 1 January 2023, so every child young enough to be listed for it is eligible); MR and OPV up to 5 years; DPT boosters up to 7 years. A child who never received Penta-3 before age 1 therefore never gets DPT-B1/DPT-B2 on this list — tell the ANM/MO, who decides the catch-up. HepB-0 can only be listed on the day of birth, so with a register filled up to yesterday it never appears. JE vaccine is not listed because Chandrapuri is not a JE-endemic district (IMM-2.4). Vitamin A, Td at 10 and 16 years and HPV are given through other channels and are not on this list.

## VIS-4 Newborns: home visits

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-4.1 HBNC visit days
Babies whose age today is 42 days or less get home visits on fixed days (HBNC-1.1). The day of birth counts as day 1, so the visit for day *d* falls on date of birth + (*d* − 1) days. List at most one HBNC item per baby:
1. Take the **latest scheduled visit dated on or before today**. If it is **not** recorded in `hbnc_visits_done`, list it: date before today = **overdue**, date today = **due_today**. (Older missed visits are not listed separately; this one replaces them.)
2. Otherwise (it was done, or no visit is dated on or before today yet), take the **next** scheduled visit dated after today. If its date is within the next 6 days and it is not recorded as done, list it as **due_this_week**. The item is written `HBNC-D<day>`, for example `HBNC-D7`. The register does not record caesarean deliveries, so every institutional delivery follows the institutional schedule below.

| Place of delivery | Visit days |
|---|---|
| institution | 3,7,14,21,28,42 |
| home | 1,3,7,14,21,28,42 |

## VIS-5 Children 6–59 months and NCD patients

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-5.1 Who is high-risk
High-risk members get **priority 1** for every one of their items that is overdue or due today (all items of that member, not only the item linked to the risk) (see VIS-6.1). Extra low-birth-weight visits (HBNC-1.2) are not on this list. A member is high-risk if any of these is true:
- a pregnant woman whose last recorded Hb is below 7 g/dL (severe anaemia, ANC-3.2) or whose last ANC blood pressure is 140/90 or more (systolic 140 or more, or diastolic 90 or more; ANC-4.1);
- a baby 42 days old or younger (newborn period, HBNC-1.1);
- a child aged 184–1824 days whose last MUAC is below 11.5 cm or who has bilateral pitting oedema (`Y`) (NUT-1.2);
- an NCD patient (HTN, DM or both) whose last recorded BP is 140/90 or more (NCD-2.1).

| Threshold | Value |
|---|---|
| pregnancy_hb_below_gdl | 7 |
| systolic_at_or_above | 140 |
| diastolic_at_or_above | 90 |
| muac_below_cm | 11.5 |
| newborn_age_max_days | 42 |

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-5.2 MUAC check
Children 6 to 59 months old are re-measured with the MUAC tape every 30 days (NUT-1.1) [block rule]. Item `MUAC-check` is due 30 days after `last_muac_date`. If the child has never been measured, it is due on the day the child becomes 184 days old. A child is considered for this item if their age today is at most 1824 days and at least 178 days (so a child turning 184 days old within the next 6 days is listed as due_this_week). It becomes overdue 28 days after its due date.

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-5.3 NCD follow-up
Patients with `ncd_condition` HTN get `BP-followup`; patients with DM get `Sugar-followup`; HTN+DM get both (NCD-2.1: BP and blood sugar every month). Each is due 30 days after the last recorded check (`last_bp_check_date` or `last_sugar_check_date`) and becomes overdue 28 days after its due date. If no check date is recorded, the follow-up is overdue.

## VIS-6 Priority

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
text:
### VIS-6.1 Priority tiers
- **Priority 1** — overdue or due_today items for a **high-risk** member (VIS-5.1). Visit these first.
- **Priority 2** — all other overdue or due_today items.
- **Priority 3** — due_this_week items (upcoming), for everyone.

Danger signs are never left for the visit list: if anyone has a danger sign, refer immediately (ESC-1.1).

doc_title: VIS — Daily Visit List Rules (Chandrapuri Block)
section_title: What the list file looks like
text:
### VIS-6.2 What the list file looks like
One row per member and item: `member_id, due_item, priority` (you may add more columns such as status; they are ignored by the scorer). Members with nothing due have no row. Item codes are exactly as written in this document (`ANC-2`, `Td-2`, `HRP-followup`, `Penta-3`, `HBNC-D7`, `MUAC-check`, `BP-followup`, `Sugar-followup`, ...).
